sentences.text: Toyotamaphimeia was a large crocodylian that measured between 6.3 and 7.3 meters in length.
Its skull was triangular and longirostrine, measuring over one meter from the tip of the premaxilla to the back of the parietal bone.
Fossil evidence reveals healed fractures in the tibia, fibula, and mandible, alongside healing bite marks on osteoderms.
This animal lived at the northern thermal limit for crocodilians in Japan.
The first fossils were found on May 3, 1964, while construction workers built a new school at Osaka University.
Researchers suggest the healed injuries on the holotype specimen may have resulted from intraspecific fights and possibly indicate it was a male.
Toyotamaphimeia is classified within the family Gavialidae, though its exact placement is sometimes noted as uncertain.
Morphological studies classify it as a basal member of Gavialinae, related to Penghusuchus and Hanyusuchus.
The fossil record spans from the Piacenzian to the Chibanian, between 3.6 and 0.129 million years ago.
It lived in Japan and Taiwan during the Middle Pleistocene.
It is debated whether Toyotamaphimeia originated in Japan or Taiwan, with some researchers arguing it evolved in Taiwan and migrated north.
